https://visegradinsight.eu/citizens-are-.text: Commentary Democratic Security Think Tank Citizens Are First in Line Against Russia’s Sabotage in CEE No time to let one's guard down in Central and Eastern Europe 21 July 2026 Resilient Futures Fellow Clear legal obligations and public awareness campaigns will embolden citizens to report suspicious activities. How to build an effective system of cooperation between authorities and citizens in reporting suspicious activities? The EU governments should: Raise awareness of the nature and scope of grey-zone activities Inspire civic engagement through targeted channels and messaging Actively utilise and proliferate technologies that power the reporting The urgency is now clear On 20 July 2026 Lithuania’s Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas publicly warned that Poland and the Baltic states may become Russia’s ‘nearest target’ for escalation due to Moscow’s failure over Ukraine. The minister’s words supported an intelligence assessment earlier cited by President Gitanas Nausėda. In recent weeks, multiple news outlets have warned that Russia may seek to test NATO’s resolve through limited kinetic actions against NATO’s eastern flank, while remaining below the threshold that would trigger a collective response under Article 5 of the Treaty. The warnings have included scenarios, like drone and missile-related provocations , false flag operations , as well as border incursions . Since 2014, Poland and the Baltic states have invested heavily in preparing for potential Russian grey zone aggression. Yet the scale and diversity of such activities observed across Europe in recent years illustrate that public security and military services alone can no longer effectively monitor and identify every suspicious act that may undermine democratic resilience and threaten national security. As a result, the wider civilian society needs to play a more active role. Grey zone attacks in Europe Until 2022 Russia relied heavily on intelligence operatives working under diplomatic cover – officially posted in embassies, consulates, and trade missions – to conduct espionage, sabotage, and other forms of malign grey zone activity across Europe. Following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, many European countries have ousted such ‘diplomats’. According to the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine, by October 2025 up to 700 Russian operatives had been expelled , including 58 from Poland alone. Deprived of this traditional infrastructure, Moscow has since adapted its operational playbook and has turned to recruiting local actors to carry out grey-zone activities across the continent. At least 151 grey zone incidents linked to Russia have been confirmed between February 2022 and February 2026, with 31 of them occurring in Poland. In November 2025, Railway explosions southeast of Warsaw placed the lives of nearly 500 people at risk. A year earlier, a parcel bomb plot which was carried out by a locally recruited proxy who dispatched four incendiary packages came close to triggering a major aviation disaster. Clearly, the threat is not abstract. Critical infrastructure facilities are particularly vulnerable to kinetic activities that fall short of direct aggression. This demands a whole-of-society approach built on civil-military cooperation. Given the scale of grey zone incidents in CEE, it is worth assessing how civilian populations are able to recognise and report such activities, as well as the extent to which citizens feel responsible for contributing to public security. Awareness and willingness to report grey zone activities According to a survey conducted by the University of Latvia, a substantial portion of respondents across the Baltic capitals believe they already personally contribute to national security. Agreement with the statement that individuals are doing enough to keep their country safe reached 53 per cent in Vilnius, 65 per cent in Riga, and 72 per cent in Tallinn. Awareness levels also appear relatively high, with roughly two-thirds of the residents in the Baltic capitals reporting that they understand what constitutes critical infrastructure. Similarly, large majorities – 78 per cent of respondents in Riga, 80 per cent in Tallinn, and 92 per cent in Vilnius – would consider photographing, filming, or observing critical infrastructure or a military facility as suspicious activity. However, willingness to report such activities reveals notable demographic divides. In Riga, for instance, 76 per cent of Latvian respondents view drawing pro-Russia or anti-NATO graffiti as suspicious activity that should be reported, while only 35 per cent of Russian respondents share this assessment. Gender disparities are also evident: in Tallinn, 77 per cent of men report understanding what critical infrastructure facilities are, compared to just 55 per cent of women. These disparities across demographic groups highlight the need for targeted and evidence-based policy responses. Source: University of Latvia Legal obligation or public awareness? So, what is the most appropriate way to engage citizens in reporting suspicious activities? Should governments adopt a more coercive approach – similar to legal obligations requiring individuals to report witnessed crimes? This was the guiding question of the legal foresight prepared within the Resilient Futures Fellowship programme 2026. The brief emphasises the importance of fostering a strong sense of moral responsibility, combined with significantly improved public awareness of activities that may carry serious implications for national security. In this approach, citizens are not treated merely as passive observers bound by legal duty, but as active participants in safeguarding democratic resilience. Download the full brief An effective framework would therefore combine clear reporting channels with practical, behaviour-based guidance. It would strengthen internal reporting obligations for providers of critical services, invest in employee training, and ensure the availability of confidential reporting options. Crucially, authorities must also close the feedback loop – demonstrating that reports are taken seriously, handled professionally and genuinely contribute to security outcomes. This translates into several concrete steps: The governments must raise public awareness about the evolving and complex nature of the threat landscape. Citizens cannot report what they do not recognise, and grey-zone activities are becoming ever more sophisticated. Authorities should actively encourage civic engagement through targeted information campaigns, drawing on models such as ‘see something, say something’ . User-friendly and trustworthy technological solutions should be developed to enable both open and anonymous reporting, incorporate safeguards against abuse, including malicious or false submissions, and ensure that reporters receive timely and meaningful feedback. Resilient Futures Fellow Roberts Kits is a Resilient Futures Fellow 2026 at Visegrad Insight. He is a researcher at the Latvian Strategy and Economic Research Institute (LaSER Think Tank) and a doctoral researcher at the University of Latvia, focusing on defence innovation, regional security, and societal resilience. His recent publications explore defence cooperation in the Baltic region and the evolving architecture of civil defence. https://www.wogx.com/news/violent-mexica.text: Tampa federal agents help capture cartel members Federal agents based in Tampa helped capture four members of a dangerous Mexican drug cartel in an operation that spanned the Globe. The defendants conspired to bring massive amounts of meth and fentanyl into the U.S. FOX 13's Kylie Jones reports. The Brief Four Jalisco New Generation Cartel members face federal charges in Tampa after an alleged scheme that involved buying military weapons with fentanyl and methamphetamine trafficked into the United States. Federal prosecutors accuse the suspects of trying to acquire machine guns, mortar launchers and grenade launchers in the Czech Republic. Lopez Velasco and Alvarado Morales made their initial court appearances Monday in Tampa, while Diaz Jimenez and Gaxiola Lopez await extradition from Europe, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office. TAMPA, Fla. - Four members of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel, one of Mexico's most powerful and violent drug organizations, are facing federal charges after they were arrested in the Czech Republic. The men are accused of trying to buy military weapons with drugs trafficked into the United States, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office. The charges were announced by U.S. Attorney Greg Kehoe during a news conference Tuesday at the U.S. Attorney's Office in downtown Tampa . The indictment accuses the four men of conspiring to traffic drugs and firearms as part of their alleged affiliation with the Jalisco New Generation Cartel, or CJNG. The U.S. Department of State has designated the Jalisco New Generation Cartel, or CJNG, as a foreign terrorist organization. Mexican cartel members arrested What we know: According to the indictment, these four cartel members face the following charges: Edgar Alejandro Lopez Velasco, 44, of Mexico: conspiracy to commit narco-terrorism, conspiracy to provide material support to terrorism, drug importation conspiracy and firearms trafficking conspiracies. Noe Diaz Jimenez, 33, of Mexico: conspiracy to commit narco-terrorism, conspiracy to provide material support to terrorism, drug importation conspiracy and firearms trafficking conspiracies. Leobardo Gaxiola Lopez, also known as "Bado," 63, of Mexico: drug importation conspiracy and firearms trafficking conspiracies. Jose Miguel Alvarado Morales, 23, of Mexico: conspiracy to commit narco-terrorism, conspiracy to provide material support to terrorism, drug importation conspiracy and firearms trafficking conspiracies. All four men face up to life in federal prison if convicted, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office. Lopez Velasco and Alvarado Morales were extradited to the Middle District of Florida and made their initial court appearances Monday in Tampa. They were ordered detained, prosecutors said. Diaz Jimenez and Gaxiola Lopez are awaiting extradition from the Czech Republic, officials said. European weapons-for-drugs operation The backstory: According to the indictment, Lopez Velasco was a representative of a high-level CJNG member, while Diaz Jimenez allegedly was a fentanyl trafficker with a fentanyl laboratory in Mexico. Gaxiola Lopez allegedly was a broker for narcotics and weapons deals, while Alvarado Morales is accused of representing another high-level CJNG member. Prosecutors say that in February 2026, Lopez Velasco and Diaz Jimenez negotiated the sale of machine guns and destructive devices from the Czech Republic to Mexico. The weapons allegedly were intended to be used against rival cartels, civilians, police and military personnel in Mexico. The indictment says the weapons included European machine guns, rocket-propelled grenade launchers, mortar launchers, ammunition and other ordnance. Cartel members accused in weapons-for-drugs scheme Four members of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel, one of Mexico's most powerful and violent drug organizations, are facing federal charges after they were arrested in the Czech Republic. The men are accused of trying to buy military weapons with drugs trafficked into the United States, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office. In exchange, the defendants are accused of paying for the weapons with fentanyl and methamphetamine that was imported into the United States for distribution. All four men were arrested in the Czech Republic in June 2026, according to federal prosecutors. Mexican authorities also dismantled Diaz Jimenez's synthetic opioid laboratory in Zapopan, Jalisco, on June 12, prosecutors said. Cartel weapons deal exposed Dig deeper: Officials said CJNG is capable of producing large quantities of methamphetamine and fentanyl, much of which is allegedly smuggled and trafficked into the United States. The cartel is also accused of using military-grade weapons and drones to attack Mexican law enforcement and assassinating Mexican officials. The organization was also allegedly involved in drug trafficking, extortion, migrant smuggling and the theft of oil and minerals in Mexico. Federal law enforcement message What they're saying: "CJNG, a designated foreign terrorist organization, is killing a record number of Americans. They are a terrorist organization and will be treated as such," Terry Cole, administrator of the Drug Enforcement Administration, said. Kehoe warned international drug and weapons traffickers that federal authorities will pursue them regardless of where they operate. "For the criminals throughout the world, wherever you think you're gonna go, and wherever you think you're gonna be, and you are going to bring harm to the American people for weaponry, for drug trafficking and anything else, we will find you, we will prosecute you," Kehoe said. Kehoe says agents with the Homeland Security Task Force in Tampa helped bust this operation. "The whole idea was that the fentanyl and meth was going to come to the United States," he said. "The actual destination was going to be determined once the arms deal culminated and was paid for. They were going to pay for the weaponry with the fentanyl and meth." Ongoing asset forfeiture efforts What we don't know: Federal authorities have not disclosed the exact monetary value of the seized drugs and military weaponry. The indictment notifies the defendants that the U.S. is seeking forfeiture of all proceeds connected to the alleged crimes, and officials noted the federal investigation remains active and ongoing. The Source: The information in this story was gathered from details provided by U.S. Attorney Greg Kehoe during a news conference at the U.S. Attorney's Office in Tampa. News Crime and Public Safety
